blocks.text: A rear-axle shaft made of medium-carbon steel is quenched to a hardness of nearly 60 HRC and is brittle enough to crack when dropped. A second tempering step at the right temperature trades some of that hardness for toughness and brings it to 40 HRC. In an aluminium aircraft rib, a similar adjustment is made by ageing at 150 C for a set time. Both treatments are controlled by one idea: transformation rate rises exponentially with temperature, so time and temperature are interchangeable.

blocks.markdown: Precipitation hardening and tempering are **thermally activated** processes: atoms must diffuse for the structure to change. The rate follows an Arrhenius law, rising rapidly with absolute temperature $T$. A treatment can therefore be described by a time-temperature combination, and two different combinations can give the same result.

headers: Time to peak hardness (typical, Al-Cu alloy)
rows: Very fast; coarser precipitates and a lower peak, risk of overageing
blocks.caption: Effect of ageing temperature on the time to reach peak hardness (a typical set of values, computed with an activation energy of 130 kJ/mol).

blocks.markdown: **Ageing curves.** Hardness against log time at a fixed ageing temperature rises as fine coherent precipitates form (**underageing**), reaches a peak, and then falls as the precipitates coarsen and lose coherency (**overageing**). Raising the temperature moves the whole curve to shorter times and lowers the peak because the precipitates nucleate more sparsely and coarsen sooner. Lowering the temperature slows the process but gives a finer dispersion and a higher peak. Ageing is stopped at or near the peak (the T6 condition for many Al alloys).

blocks.caption: t1 and t2 are the times to reach the same condition (for example the peak hardness) at absolute temperatures T1 and T2; Q is the activation energy (J per mol) and R = 8.314 J per mol K.

blocks.title: Time to peak hardness at a higher ageing temperature
blocks.prompt: An aluminium alloy reaches peak hardness in 24 h at 150 C. Taking $Q=130$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, estimate the time to the same condition at 190 C.

steps.text: Convert the temperatures to kelvin: $T_1=423.15$ K and $T_2=463.15$ K, and compute $Q/R=130000/8.314=15\,636$ K.
Compute the difference in reciprocal temperatures.

blocks.answer: About 1 hour at 190 C: 40 degrees higher cuts the ageing time by a factor of 24, but the peak hardness is lower.

blocks.markdown: **Tempering.** As-quenched martensite is very hard and brittle. Heating (tempering) lets carbon diffuse out of the supersaturated martensite to form carbides, reduces the dislocation density and relieves residual stress, so hardness falls and toughness rises. Time and temperature are again interchangeable, and the **Hollomon-Jaffe parameter** collapses a (time, temperature) treatment into one number: two tempers with the same value give about the same hardness.

blocks.caption: T is the absolute temperature (K), t the time in hours and C a constant of about 20 for steels (it depends somewhat on composition). Equal H gives about equal hardness.

blocks.title: Comparing tempering treatments
blocks.prompt: With $C=20$, compare (i) 500 C for 1 h with 600 C for 1 h, and (ii) find the time at 450 C that matches 500 C for 1 h.

steps.text: Compute $H$ for the first treatment ($T=773.15$ K, $\log_{10}1=0$).
Compute $H$ for 600 C for 1 h ($T=873.15$ K); it is larger, so the steel is more tempered and softer.
For equal $H$ at 450 C ($T=723.15$ K), solve for the logarithm of time.
Convert the logarithm to a time.

blocks.answer: 600 C for 1 h is tempered far more than 500 C for 1 h; 24 h at 450 C is equivalent to 1 h at 500 C.

headers: Hardness of 0.45 wt% C steel (HRC, typical, illustrative)
rows: Avoid 260 to 370 C for toughness (tempered martensite embrittlement)
Good balance of strength and toughness
blocks.caption: Tempering curve of a medium-carbon steel; values are typical and for orientation only.

blocks.markdown: **Specifying a schedule.** To reach a target hardness in a medium-carbon steel: (1) **austenitise** at about 30 to 50 C above $A_{c3}$ (typically 840 C for a 0.45 % C steel) long enough to dissolve the carbides; (2) **quench** quickly enough to avoid pearlite and bainite, so the structure is martensite; (3) **temper** at the temperature that gives the target hardness on the tempering curve, then cool. Avoid the embrittlement ranges (about 260 to 370 C and, for slowly cooled steels with P or Sb impurities, about 375 to 575 C, where a quick cool or Mo addition is used).

blocks.title: Selecting a tempering temperature
blocks.prompt: A 0.45 wt% C steel shaft is quenched to martensite and must be tempered to 36 HRC. Use the tempering curve to specify the schedule.

steps.text: The target 36 HRC lies between 500 C (38 HRC) and 600 C (30 HRC), so interpolate linearly: the slope is $-8$ HRC per 100 C, i.e. $-0.08$ HRC per C.
Austenitise at 840 C for about 30 min, quench in oil to below 100 C so that no pearlite or bainite forms, and temper at 525 C for 1 h.
After tempering, cool rapidly (for example in air or oil) through 375 to 575 C if the steel is susceptible to temper embrittlement.

blocks.answer: Austenitise at 840 C, oil quench, temper at about 525 C for 1 h to obtain about 36 HRC.

blocks.title: Tempering curves are not unique
blocks.text: A tempering curve applies to a given composition, section and time (here 1 h). Alloy elements such as Cr and Mo shift it to higher temperature (secondary hardening), and a different time must be compensated using the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter. For critical parts, always verify the hardness after heat treatment.

points: Ageing hardness rises to a peak as fine coherent precipitates form and then falls on overageing; higher ageing temperature shortens the time to peak, following an Arrhenius law, and gives a lower peak.
The Hollomon-Jaffe parameter $H=T(C+\log_{10}t)$, with $C\approx20$, gives the same tempered hardness for equal $H$; temperature has a much stronger effect than time.
A heat-treatment schedule for a medium-carbon steel is austenitise, quench to martensite, then temper at the temperature read from the tempering curve for the target hardness.

questions.stem: A precipitation-hardening alloy is aged at a higher temperature than normal. Compared with the normal treatment, which change is expected?

options.text: The peak hardness is reached later but at a higher value
The peak is reached at the same time but is lower
The peak hardness is reached sooner but at a lower value
Hardness continues to rise for an unlimited time

questions.correctOptionText: The peak hardness is reached sooner but at a lower value

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: a lower temperature gives a later and higher peak.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: time to peak changes exponentially with temperature.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: faster diffusion shortens the time to the peak, but the precipitates coarsen sooner and the peak is lower.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: after the peak the alloy overages and softens.

questions.explanation: The Arrhenius law makes the reaction faster at a higher temperature, so the peak is reached in less time. The precipitates are coarser and more widely spaced at the peak, so the maximum hardness is lower.

questions.stem: What happens to hardness in an alloy that is held for a long time at its ageing temperature, well beyond the peak hardness?

options.text: The precipitates coarsen and lose coherency, so hardness falls (overageing)
Hardness continues to increase because more precipitate forms
Hardness stays at the peak, since precipitation has ended
The alloy returns to the supersaturated solid solution

questions.correctOptionText: The precipitates coarsen and lose coherency, so hardness falls (overageing)

distractorRationale.a: Correct: coarsening increases the spacing between particles, so dislocations bypass them more easily.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: after the peak the volume fraction is nearly complete and coarsening dominates.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the peak is a maximum that is not maintained.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: re-solution needs a temperature near the solvus, not the ageing temperature.

questions.explanation: Beyond the peak, small particles dissolve and larger ones grow, so the number of obstacles falls and their spacing grows. The yield strength and hardness therefore decrease, which is why ageing is stopped at the peak (T6).

questions.stem: An aluminium alloy reaches its peak hardness in 10 h at 160 C. The activation energy for the process is 120 kJ mol$^{-1}$ ($R=8.314$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$). Using $t_2=t_1\exp[(Q/R)(1/T_2-1/T_1)]$, estimate the time to the same condition at 190 C, in hours.
questions.explanation: With $T_1=433.15$ K and $T_2=463.15$ K the difference in reciprocals is $0.0021592-0.0023087=-1.495\times10^{-4}$ K$^{-1}$, and $Q/R=14\,434$ K. The exponent is $-2.158$, so $t_2=10\times\exp(-2.158)=10\times0.1156=1.16$ h.

questions.stem: What does the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter $H=T(C+\log_{10}t)$ tell the engineer about two tempering treatments?

options.text: Treatments with equal values give the same hardness only if their temperatures are equal
The treatment with the longer time is always the softer
It gives the exact hardness in HRC without a tempering curve
Treatments with equal values give about the same hardness, and a change in temperature has a much larger effect than a change in time

questions.correctOptionText: Treatments with equal values give about the same hardness, and a change in temperature has a much larger effect than a change in time

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: equal H with different temperatures and times gives about the same hardness.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the product depends on the temperature as well as the time, and a higher temperature for a shorter time may be softer.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: the parameter indicates equivalence, not absolute hardness.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the parameter combines time and temperature, with temperature dominant because time enters through a logarithm.

questions.explanation: The parameter is proportional to the absolute temperature and to the logarithm of time. Multiplying the time by 10 adds only $T$ to $H$, whereas raising the temperature by 50 K adds about 1000, so temperature dominates.

questions.stem: A steel is tempered for 2 h at 550 C. Using $H=T(20+\log_{10}t)$ with $T$ in kelvin and $t$ in hours, what is the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter?

options.text: About 11 200
About 16 700
About 18 100
About 17 000

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this uses the Celsius temperature instead of kelvin.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: this adds 2 instead of the logarithm of 2.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: this uses the natural logarithm in place of the base-10 logarithm.

questions.explanation: The temperature in kelvin is 823.15 K, and $\log_{10}2=0.301$, so the bracket is 20.301. The product is $823.15\times20.301=16\,711$.

questions.stem: A steel tempered at 540 C for 1 h has the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter $H=T(20+\log_{10}t)$ with $T$ in kelvin and $t$ in hours. At what time, in hours, would a temper at 480 C give the same parameter?
questions.explanation: The reference is $H=813.15\times20=16\,263$. At 480 C ($T=753.15$ K), $20+\log_{10}t=16263/753.15=21.594$, so $\log_{10}t=1.594$ and $t=10^{1.594}=39.2$ h. Lowering the temperature by 60 C therefore requires nearly forty times the time.

questions.stem: A 0.45 wt% C steel is quenched and must be tempered to 41 HRC. The tempering curve (1 h) gives 44 HRC at 400 C and 38 HRC at 500 C. Assuming linear behaviour between these points, find the tempering temperature, in degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: The hardness falls by $44-38=6$ HRC over 100 C, so 0.06 HRC per C. To fall from 44 to 41 HRC requires $3/0.06=50$ C, so $T=400+50=450$ C.

questions.stem: A shaft of medium-carbon steel must have both high strength and good toughness. Which sequence of heat treatments is correct?

options.text: Temper first, then austenitise and quench
Quench from below the eutectoid temperature and then age
Austenitise and cool slowly in the furnace, then temper
Austenitise, quench to martensite, then temper at the temperature that gives the target hardness

questions.correctOptionText: Austenitise, quench to martensite, then temper at the temperature that gives the target hardness

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: tempering is applied to martensite, so it must follow the quench.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: quenching from below the eutectoid temperature does not give martensite.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: furnace cooling gives pearlite and ferrite, which tempering would not change.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: martensite forms on quenching and tempering then trades hardness for toughness.

questions.explanation: A quench from the austenite region forms hard, brittle martensite. Tempering then lets carbon precipitate as carbides and relieves stress, so the final hardness is set by the tempering temperature and time.

questions.stem: Describe how ageing time and ageing temperature affect the hardness of a precipitation-hardened alloy, and explain the form of the hardness-time curve and why a higher ageing temperature gives a lower peak.
markingGuide: Hardness rises with time as fine coherent precipitates form and obstruct dislocations (underageing)
Peak hardness corresponds to a dense dispersion of small precipitates and the optimum particle size
Beyond the peak, precipitates coarsen and become incoherent, the spacing grows, and dislocations bypass them, so hardness falls (overageing)
Higher temperature increases diffusion rate exponentially (Arrhenius), so the peak is reached sooner
At higher temperature the precipitates are fewer and coarser at the peak, so peak hardness is lower; lower temperature gives a higher peak but takes longer
Industrial ageing is chosen to give the peak (T6) in a practical time
questions.explanation: Ageing is thermally activated, so temperature controls both the speed and the scale of the precipitate dispersion. Fine, dense precipitates give the maximum obstruction to slip, which is why a low temperature favours a higher peak.

questions.stem: A 0.45 wt% C steel shaft must be hardened to 40 HRC. Specify a complete heat-treatment schedule (austenitising, quench, temper), justify each step, and use the Hollomon-Jaffe parameter with $C=20$ to find how long a temper at 480 C would take to match 1 h at 450 C. Use the tempering curve: 44 HRC at 400 C and 38 HRC at 500 C.
markingGuide: Austenitise at about 840 C (30 to 50 C above Ac3) so all carbides dissolve to austenite
Quench in oil or water fast enough to avoid pearlite and bainite, giving martensite (about 58 HRC)
Temper: interpolating, 40 HRC lies between 44 at 400 C and 38 at 500 C, so about 400 + (44-40)/0.06 = 467 C (about 470 C)
Rapid cooling after the temper if the steel is susceptible to temper embrittlement, and avoiding 260 to 370 C
Concludes that temperature has a much greater effect than time
questions.explanation: Hardening needs martensite, which tempering converts to a stable microstructure of fine carbides in ferrite; the hardness is controlled by the temper. The Hollomon-Jaffe parameter shows that a small increase in temperature allows a large decrease in time.
